When Mirror's Edge was just released, the developers were still planning to scale it, fill the game with life it was entitled to. But that never happened. So what we have for our money now is a very original project, both visually and technically, with the very well-performed parkour movement system, plus fluid combat system, plus the very natural-looking city environment to do all those fantastic tricks that game is so full of. However, it is really hurt to see all the shortcomings, where the developers never had enough time to make the game they were planning initially. This starts with the major things like the story, which is way too short and sketchy, and can only fit some early teenager comic book fans. There are way too many gaps and logic failures from all the characters, in the events that average player will see in just 5 hours... Also, the devs left unfinished most of the secondary, but still important tasks. Like the model of Faith's sister, who'll be "detained" right until the very last game sequence in her police uniform, with all the stuff like radio, cuffs and baton, still on her belt.

But the main shortcoming of this wonderful game is not the story itself. Neither is those nasty little things none can't fix until it's all cut. No, the main problem is the game pace. Of course, it's very fun to run across the roofs of the town. Making the surface work for you. But... 90%+ of layouts on the game levels have only one valid point to continue your movement. It's really restraining when you know all your possible special powers and just has to use them in a very strictly defined order: there we go with the horizontal wall run, there we use slide and there - jump...  Sure, we can vary some basic movements on the easy routs, but every time when the developers adding a big puzzle, it has only one proper way to climb it. Or two ways, but only on some very special occasions. Oh, and when you've made some really long chain of stunts, usually it is good to step back a bit, do some other things, like talking, walking, behaving like the ordinary citizen for a while... Never-ending action gets boring as the adrenaline wears off.

Mirror's Edge is very fluid and alluring game, it's generally good in all what it does, except the story background for all those roofs runs. Visuals and sounds in the game deserve the highest praise, the controls are quite good, except for the few QTE sequences. Apart from some of the high kicks, especially in cutscenes, the combat system is very realistic and cool, many thanks to those who were involved in the motion capture and programming it.

All in all, I'd give Mirror's Edge 7/10 mark. Yes, the game is very nice, yes, I had a blast with that first-person-view feeling when you are jumping from one roof to another. But it wears off a bit faster than I would hope to. I would love to see all that in some other, more sophisticated game, some shooter like Syndicate, some action-RPG like Deus Ex... Maybe Thief game could have been better in some cross-breed with Mirror's Edge, I don't know. It's just... some taste of incompleteness in that complete game. And Mirror's Edge Catalyst ain't exactly much better, just more of the same. So, technically, a great game. But that runners' show... too flat.

There is something special about this game. For me it's not the parkour perse, and not even the storyline... But there is just something appealing that this game has. The environment, the vibes, the soundtrack... It's just so nice.

Mirror's Edge is a game I've wanted to play for a while, and this past week I've completed it over once. Is it worth playing? Yes.

From creators DICE (known for work on the Battlefield series and the 2015 Star Wars Battlefront), Mirror's Edge is a first-person platformer which involves parkour in all its glory, leaping across buildings, scaling walls, and traversing up factories. Parkour functions very smoothly, and the first-person view adds a layer of immersion which helps to sell the games atmosphere. Say what you want about the plot and characters (I found both to be good enough), this game's setting is a unique piece of art. Taking place sometime in the future in an unidentified utopian city controlled by a totalitarian government, Mirror's Edge conveys this by its very simplistic and pleasant art style: White everywhere, with bold colours such as brick red, lime green, or saphiere blue alongside. Cutscenses are also presented in a unqiue "drawing animation" (search up the first cutscene, I can't really explain it well), with a charm of their own. The soundtrack is also quite amazing, all the way from the main theme "Still Alive" to more atmospheric tracks used in the levels.

As for gameplay, this game is centered around parkour as I said before. Your moveset includes jumping (no duh), sliding, wall running, climbing, and clambering to name a few. The feeling of successfully pulling of multiple moves at a fast pace is incredibly rewarding, and the game is entirely hard to master. Difficultly (for parkour) progression is smooth throughout the entire game, and (at least for me) the game never felt cheap at any times. However, combat also is an important part of this game. In some sections enemy soldiers will attack you, and you'll have to use kicks and punches to either kill or unarm them, in order to use their weapons. Gunplay in this game is very basic (kind of surprising as this game comes from DICE), and only serves as a way to kill baddies faster. Weapons include SMG's, shotguns, and snipers, however you wont find yourself using them too often as the bulk of the game is parkour, and some sections with enemies do involve chases, which are awesome and tense.

That's pretty much this game! Sound a bit basic for you? Well, the main campaign/story mode is only 5 hours (it might take you shorter), and besides that there's a time trial mode, but that's pretty much the game. While a piece of art IMO, the game could have used a few more levels for the story mode, and perhaps a race mode for multiplayer, or at least something related to that. Gunplay/combat could also be expanded, and the parkour moveset could always be refined and expanded upon. Overall, it's an awesome concept and an original idea for a game, and I would give it a 7.5/10. For $19.99 it's a good price if you are absolutely sold on this game, but either than that I would either be cautious or wait for a price drop due to the lack of much content. 

Also, Mirror's Edge 2 for 2016!

Yes, I have 20 hours in this game. But first, some background.

Like with Final Fantasy XIII and Remember Me, I avoided this game because people complained about it when it came out despite me being hyped for it. I bought it when it was on sale for a dollar and regret not buying it day-of.

I can see where people can find significant flaws, especially playing now just before the new game comes out, but there's so much good in this game that I think it's okay to overlook. The story's a little undercooked, Merc annoys the hell out of me (the white guy who's talking in your ear for 90% of the game), and for such an important character, you see Faith's sister three times and she does nothing significant. The borderless cartoon animation comic-wannabe cutscenes between levels are tragic and make my heart hurt. The biggest complaint I've seen is also slightly true: yes, some jumps and parkour tricks can be difficult to pull off because of finicky controls and poor item interaction (like not being in the correct centimeter length from a pipe so you fall to your death despite staring right at the bloody thing).

But, honestly, the only parts of the game I got truly and genuinely frustrated at were the fights (particularly one boss fight with a ninja person *spoiler spoiler*). Thank god Catalyst ditched the guns because wow, I didn't get this game to play a shooter.

Despite all of this, which I guess some is enough to ruin this game for people, I cannot recommend this game enough. It is quite possibly one of my favorite games of all time, and I play a lot of games. I spent $200 on Catalyst and got the prequel graphic novel. I own the soundtrack to the first game and will probably get the next. I seriously love this game. So what's good?

It's art, pure and simple. And there's nothing else like it. Maybe some indie stuff popped up in hopes of scratching that virtual parkour itch, but nothing really compares to this full game of jumps and swings. It's like making Assassin's Creed first person and giving you complete control of every wall dash, every jump, every lunge, all those little tricky grabs and spins, and turning travel into the puzzle rather than combat or hacking minigames. Every tiny detail is carefully created and placed to challenge you and force you to think creatively, using the tools you learn in the tutorial on increasingly difficult puzzles. Even the fights can sometimes be enjoyable when you treat it as a marathon instead of an fps shooting gallery.

The game is gorgeous, even for today's standards (though Faith's model is a little choppy). The color contrast and choice in neon vibrance and bright white have been lauded for years now. And it always stands our, no matter how many times you play the game. In a world of greys and browns, this game is quite the visual gem and that can't be understated. Traveling over skyscrapers really shows all these contrasts, then busting into office buildings and cunstruction sites, subways and malls, put those big blues, oranges, and greens right in your face.

I'm a huge cyberpunk fan and there's not a lot of it. People want to think it died in the '80s, but I say fuck that. Even if we don't have AIs or cyberspace, this is cyberpunk. A small group of rebels try to circumnavigate the system that the ruling totalitatarian government has created in this near-future dystopia. It's guilded, with high-rises and men in swanky suits, but crime and death in the cracks. This point's more about my personal interests, but anything cyberpunk is a win in my book.

The music perfectly frames everything going on. It's fast, it's calm, and it's creepy. People complain about "Still Alive" but I'm one of the nerds who loves that fucking song. When i heard the composer for the main soundtrack was coming back, I immediately got the collector's for Catalyst. He's good. It's soft, kinda futuristic (as we'd like to imagine it) and is the perfect audial counterpart to the colorful visuals.

Then there's time trials and doing speedruns of actual levels from the game, which is always fun. There's hackers on the pc, so don't bother trying to be number one on the leaderboards, but it can be very fun to push yourself to beat your own best times. Some of the most fun I had in this game was discovering new and faster ways of completing levels, like trick jumps I missed on my initial run or near-glitches that let you skip whle sections. I suppose these types of things exist in all sorts of games, but it truly feels different in a game with the parkour gameplay like this. I also thought the voice-acting was well done, particularly on faith and Jacknife, even Merc (despite me loathing his voice).

I am a very big fan of this game, now franchise, and will likely love it forever. No, it's not perfect. If it was, would we need a sequel? But it's unique, fun, and stays in your brain. Granted, the folks around here bashing on it aren't likely to think about it again, but how are you to know you won't love it until you try it?

One scene will always stick with me. Faith's sister's first appearance is in a cutscene, and not one with that horrible cartoon animation, but a realtime in-game cutscene in first person. There aren't a lot of these (in fact, off the top of my head, I can only remember two). This one is a good length, the vast city is visible in the background, you don't have control over Faith's actions, and it's emotional. It sets up the plot for the game (which isn't dreadful, they just could've done al ot more with it) and the relationship between Faith and her sister. Faith's personality is on full display here, her drive to run and escape problems rather than face them, and we never see her face. Many fps games don't have cutscenes from first person where the first-person character actually does stuff that the player doesn't do. But it's not awkward, it doesn't feel weird, even when the two sisters embrace and you see Kate's head go over Faith's shoulder. It's fluid and makes me wish there were more of these throughout the game. Even outside of the parkour, the music, and the visuals, this style of cutscene will always stick with me.

TLDR- I love it, you might, there's problems, what game doesn't? You won't know if you're a hater or a lover until you try it. There's running, jumping, music, some iffy storytelling, and an overall unique experience. I've also heard it's good with VR. Give it a shot, it may just be your next obsession.

Not sure what to make of Mirror's Edge.  I got it on the cheap, and don't regret paying a couple of quid for it. And it's a game I've been meaning to have a look at for years. But having finished it I'm not convinced it's as good as its reputation.

Mirror's Edge is a running-and-jumping game, at heart, and its appeal is the speed and fluidity with which you can move through its environments. The emphasis here has to be on 'can', though: when the parkour elements come together, the experience is joyous, almost sublime; but these moments when things cohere are quite rare. This is partly because the controls are janky, and your character (Faith) often does things you don't want her to. But it's also a result of the level design, which quite perversely often seems to want you to move through the environments in a stop-start fashion, thus losing momentum. Mirror's Edge is probably a game one could get really good at, and if I were better at it than I am some of these problems wouldn't be so pronounced. But nothing I saw in the game made me want to practice, or even replay it at all. So much for skill.

The other element of the gameplay is combat, which is awful. You can punch/kick, you can disarm, and you can shoot, and all three of these things are badly implemented. There's also a bullet-time thing, which as far as I can see was put in to mitigate the crappiness of the other combat mechanics. Combat adds nothing to what is enjoyable about this game, and even detracts from it. It is possible just to run/jump past most enemies, and you don't have to kill anyone, but your life will be harder if you don't bludgeon the odd copper in your rooftop odyssey. All in all, it's tempting to think the game would be much better without the fighting; but then it would seem like a glorified tech demo (and, crepuscular reader, my suspicion is that Mirror's Edge /is/ a glorified tech demo). The bad combat compounds the weaknesses of the running and jumping - having to stop moving in order to indulge in a bit of al fresco police brutality really kicks you out of the flow.

There are some great things. The visual style is really singular, and the graphics still look great all these years later. The music is another highlight - cybersounds for a future-dystopic age. At its best Mirror's Edge is totally immersive - you'll feel physically dizzy as you leap over a two-hundred foot drop, your body will lean into a wall as Faith scampers along it, defying gravity. It's the sort of thing VR was made for (not that I'd know).

There's a story, but its pretty boilerplate - corrupt law-enforcement, plucky antiheroes, you know the score. The setting, an unspecified city in the near future (or what was the near future in 2009) is serviceable if a bit bland. There's a kind of Singapore vibe - hypermodern, authoritarian city-state - which is nice. There are (I think) nine missions plus a tutorial, but not a huge amount of variety or game-progression, and overall it's very short. It took me about five hours to go from beginning to end, and I play games relatively slowly, so this is a thin offering. Again, if you got really into it, and wanted to hone your skills to perfection in the time-trial mode, you might get a lot more play-time out of it, but in short I can't be bothered. Mirror's Edge is probably worth trying if on sale and you're curious, but in the final analysis I was disappointed.

Mirror's Edge is developed by DICE and released in 2009 for PC.
It's an original game, a sort of First Person Parkour.

The plot takes place in a huge city with no name and no soul, all dressed in white.
This dystopian society, in which information is controlled by the state, 
emphasizes surveillance and security to the hilt.
Since the usual means of communication are no longer secure,
the few who resist this quasi-totalitarian regime call on the Runners to transmit their messages.
The player takes on the role of Faith Connors, one of the city's top Runners.
Her sister Kate, has chosen a very different path, she's a policewoman.
Faith intercepts a police call reporting an attack on the offices of Robert Pope, 
a friend of her parents and favorite candidate in the upcoming mayoral election.
When Faith arrives on the scene, she finds her sister standing over Pope's dead body.
The police suspect Kate of being behind the murder, 
since she was already on the scene before the police officially intervened.
Faith must do everything in her power to escape the police and clear her sister's name.
But all she has taken with her is a meagre clue, a piece of paper marked "Icarus"...

This adventure is rather atypical in the world of shooters,
since it's a parkour game disguised as an FPS.
The gameplay is exhilarating and the atmosphere unique.
Faith is a slender, athletic and dynamic runner.
She'll have to use all her skills to deliver her documents and escape from the police.
Her best weapons are her speed and agility, the skills she needs to parkour.
She'll often have to climb over obstacles, slide under others,
jump from gutter to gutter, from building to building,
leaping from bar to bar, use zip lines over long distances,
sneak into air ducts, etc... 
She can also run through doors.

Just don't expect to kill enemies by the hundreds,
Faith isn't really a warrior, but a Runner.
She doesn't seek confrontation, preferring to run away from the threat to complete her mission.
If Faith finds herself cornered, surrounded by police, 
she can always fight back, kicking and punching.
If necessary, she can disarm the police and use their own weapons against them... 

The game is very pretty and ages very well thanks to its distinctive aesthetic.
The city's architecture is classy, with a clean, minimalist design.
Most of the buildings are white and devoid of emotion.
Advertising and interiors, on the other hand, 
feature bright colors that contrast with the clinical atmosphere of the exterior.
Lighting is beautiful, with the use of lens flare in particular.
The level design is very well conceived, and the maps are pleasant to navigate.
Thanks to the "Runner's Vision", important elements turn red as Faith approaches them.
This reveals the most accessible route to take, but it's not always the quickest.
The "Reaction Time" allows you to slow down the action 
and concentrate on what you need to do, 
and anticipate enemy movements in the event of a confrontation.

The levels are interspersed with anime-like cutscenes, very well realized and skilfully staged.
The absence of a TV series derived from the game is almost regrettable.

The soundtrack is very eclectic, and sets the perfect pace for the frantic chases between Faith and the police.
The theme "Still Alive" sung by Lisa Miskovsky is a real masterpiece.

There are, however, a few drawbacks.
Some passages in the game can prove arduous due to the absence of Quick Save.
The checkpoints are quite far apart, and some sequences can be quite frustrating.
The game is quite demanding, you'll die and retry several times.
You need good timing to carry out the action sequences with precision.
The cops are sometimes heavily armed, while others are formidable in hand-to-hand combat.
Mirror's Edge is very short, and its lifespan is artificially lengthened by its poorly balanced difficulty.
The game is limited to 62 FPS and the FOV cannot be modified.

The 2000s ended on a high note with Mirror's Edge.
Its innovative gameplay and singular artistic direction make it a highly enjoyable game.
But you'll need a lot of patience to fully appreciate it!

This game was originally released in January, 2009, and remarkably holds up well today, minus some snickering about [url=http://markholtz.info/13o]playing old games[/url]. Out of the box, the game only has a maximum frame rate of ~60 FPS and almost no Anisotropic filtering (AF). However, almost ten years later, and we have better monitors and video cards. With some modification of the config files via [url=http://markholtz.info/pcgamingwikimirrorsedge]PC Gaming Wiki[/url], I was able to increase the frame rate to well beyond my monitor’s 165 frames per second at 2560×1440 resolution.

And, it is so worth it too. The graphics are absolutely stunning in this game, with some other reviewers calling it a “beautiful game”. The music in this game is absolute fantastic too.

EA DICE, which is better known for it’s Battlefield series, released this game under a slightly different concept. Instead of being a shooter, you employ [url=http://markholtz.info/parkour]parkour[/url] as you leap from building to building to uncover an assassination conspiracy involving your sister Kate. Leap? For me, it involves falling (and failing) so many times, I’m surprised my character Faith didn’t storm off the game in protest. I think I developed a temporary aversion to heights because of this game. The creators did state that it is possible to complete the game without firing a single shot, and I admit, I got through the first several chapters using hand-to-hand combat. However, near the end, I threw up my hands and elected to use weapons.

This game normally retails for $20 on Steam, but is discounted regularly to $5. At $5, it’s a steal, and easily worth purchasing. You may end up having to purchase a new controller and mouse after you complete this game.

[i]Mirror's Edge[/i] is an action-adventure platform game developed by DICE and published by Electronic Arts.

[b]Story[/b]
Mirror's Edge is set in a near-future city where comfortable life and non-existent crime are achieved thanks to regime that controls the media and its citizens. Here there is also an underground crew of parkour couriers called Runners, who deliver private goods and sensitive information across the city to those who oppose the goverment, marking them as a threat.
You play as one of the Runners named Faith Connors, who after one of the runs finds out about her sister being framed for murder. She sets out to discover secrets hiding behind the assassination and to prove sisters innocence.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
Pretty simple deal, utilize Faith's parkour skills to navigate the city and complete levels in order to progress! Jump between rooftops, wallrun, slide down, vault over obstacles, climb and more to make your way through cities infrastructure.
Key part in successful parkour lies within momentum, as taking a moment to gather speed will let you run faster, jump farther or climb higher.
Game also features help in navigation called Runner Vision, which highlights certain objects or paths with red colour to help you find a way forward, plus to make gameplay feel smoother as you won't waste time and speed in searching where you have to go.

Of course Faith doesn't have that easy, and will have to deal with police force on her path. Game allows you to outsmart opponents and utilize parkour skills to simply pass them, but when moment comes where you are face to face with enemy, you have to get handy. You can perform melee attacks, block and counter incoming strikes, but considering most enemies doesn't want to get close and personal, you might have to reach out and disarm them.
Faith can use all firearms to kill enemies without the need to get her hands messy, yet bigger weapons than pistol not only slow her down but also prevent from performing parkour moves, forcing you to go guns blazing. Which makes sense, I haven't seen anyone yet do parkour with heavy machine gun in both hands.
So game gives you certain freedom in approach: parkour to evade, slap everyone you see or grab cold iron and use it against enemies.
Getting hit results in health loss and screen being more red than usual, with medicine for such issue being few second of no-damage-taken period when regeneration kicks in. Classic. Get too much damage and you will revisit recent checkpoint. Same applies to parkour, as screwup in a roof jump results in death...and that crunchy sound once Faith lands, or rather splatters...ughhhh, hate it.

Each level has 3 hidden yellow bags serving as collectibles, though you get nothing from collecting them, beside sense of self-acomplishment I suppose. Look for Runner's marks and search areas close to them!

[b]Playtime, replayability and other modes[/b]
It took me less than 5 hours to make through the story.
Definitely a game that has to be played twice as your first playthrough while still being enjoyable, will feature a learning curve on how to tackle levels and deal with parkour mechanics, making it feel rather rough. Second playthrough thanks to gathered experience and few hours under the belt should be simply more satisfying, seamless from gameplay perspective. Plus, you can collect useless collectible bags you might have missed out on!

Additionally you have a time trial mode with two options, both rely on parkouring your way as fast as possible and earning medals based on your time. One copies missions from the story, and second focuses on shorter sections with checkpoints you have to pass. If you love cutting miliseconds from a clock and finding most optimal way to the finish line then these modes are made for you!

[b]Pros and cons[/b]
Fantastic controls and fluid movement that make up for parkour with the addition of momentum mechanic, create immersive experience. It's pleasant, responsive and offers solid curve for those who might want to advance their skills in the game by spending more time with it to learn all the little tricks and nuances.
One cannot mention Mirror's Edge without talking about fantastic visual side it offers. Mix of sticking out white colour with primary colours used in the game, bounded by ton of soft shadows gives game a very unique artstyle that looks great even today.

As for 'mixed' element I throw in whole story, not only because presentation through animated cutscenes looks average at best but also due to few confusing plot moments. Very okay, nothing special type.

Levels themselfs also can fit into mixed category, due to them being on every side of the spectrum. While I understand game is linear, sometimes it's so restricted and on rails it just doesn't provide freedom parkour is known for. Additionally there are few moments, due to combat sections for example, where Mirror's Edge becomes a trial and error game which can lead to frustration. But there are chapters which not only feature multiple roads to avoid enemies, giving you freedom to get bit creative, they have solid variety of obstacles to create really fun parkour moments.

For negatives, combat. Not enjoyable, ruins the flow, quite ofter feeling unnecessary for the sake of padding the time and guns you can utilize are horrible from gunplay perspective. Melee is not that bad but sadly game has very few melee encounters and that is where problem lies, it focuses too much on picking up the gun and enganging in shootouts that break the pacing, rather than on swift hand-to-hand brawling.

Ultimately Mirror's Edge is all about flow. If you will quickly get into a game, get a feel of mechanics and movement, it will be a fantastic, smooth sailing experience. However if you get into that one section which makes you fail twice or thrice, you lose focus or get annoyed, or you just don't get into a game as much as you thought, it can feel like a slog, where you are not progressing naturally and have to fight tooth and nail for every checkpoint, making game not as enjoyable as some (myself included) claim. I thought opening cinematic mentioning whole "Parkour flow" deal was over exaggerating but after a playthrough I do have to take it back and fully agree.

[b]Conclusion[/b]
Fantastic visual style and well crafted parkour make Mirror's Edge a unique title definitely worth playing, even if unsatisfying combat and few "Trial and Error" moments might ruin your flow.

I finally decided to play this. What a rush! This is the sort of game that can be played ten years from now and it will still play great and look great. It's one of those timeless games.

Positives:
[list]
[*] Simple and refined gameplay, check. The free running is so very enjoyable. The sense of speed as you rush across rooftops is exhilirating. For someone like me who loves the thrill of heights, it puts a grin on my face. (You'll probably want to raise the game's FOV, it's pretty easy, look it up.) 
[*] I want to live in that city. Maybe without the dystopia but, it looks so nice. The art direction in the game is gorgeous. Indoors also. I want to work in those offices. I would desk jockey the shit out of those office environments.
[*] You can take a screenshot at any time and hang it on your wall. My F12 key is wearing out.
[*] I liked the world they created. The runner culture. The story keeps it simple, with just enough to provide you with incentive. Character designs are great too, from Faith to the runners and villains. Check out the unlockable art in the main menu.
[*] I was sad to hear Rhianna Pratchett wasn't invited to write Mirror's Edge 2 because  I liked her take on this. A girl on the wrong side of the law who's doing everything to save her her sister, the framed cop. Interesting backstory to the city and the characters. I'd love an animated series with the same setting and aesthetics.
[/list] 


The negatives:
[list]
[*] Combat is definitely the weak point of the game. Most of the time it's frustrating. Lots of people wish it didn't have combat at all. I think they could have made it work. You can disarm most enemies via quicktime events that suck, even if you use the slowmo button.
[*] For a game about free running, it's pretty damn linear. I've seen corridor shooters that offered more varied paths. At least I played it without "runner vision" which literally paints your path in red.
[*] I didn't mind these but it seems a lot of people did: the cutscene cartoons are not as well made as the rest of the game. Not a big deal for me.
[/list]

Mirror's Edge 2 is supposed to address these issues, if it ever releases. DICE are a hostage to developing Battlefield after Battlefield, sadly. Unique and fresh games like Mirror's Edge are an exception and a rarity.

Mirror's Edge, when it launched, was a phenomenon - it gave you the freedom, with its unique movement system, to more or less pick your path to your system. Prince of Persia may have hinted, but this game was the first to do it properly and base the entire gameplay experience around movement.

You play as Faith, a Runner in a dystopian future, which ironically enough mimics our modern world in some way (mass surveillance, as an example). You run, jump, slide, swing and occasionally all of those together to reach your destination (momentum is the key). The fluidity of the system is incredible, not to mention a beautifully pristine game world (the colours and architecture are still amongst the best I have seen). The campaign is short, but the time trial modes and additional difficulties will keep you entertained for hours.

To those who complain about the gunplay - this is not a shooter and guns are not the focal point. That being said, it can be a bit tricky to use the weapons, and at certain points you make life much more difficult for yourself (unnecessarily so) if you choose not to pick up a gun and shoot. For the most part, your intention is to either avoid or disarm the opposition, not attempt to engage in gunfights.

Mirror's Edge is a game that truly pushes the boundaries of what a first-person action game can achieve. Released on PC in 2009, it was praised for its immersive atmosphere, vast vertical and horizontal spaces, fluid game dynamics, and natural camera mechanics that follow the character's movements.

One of the standout features of Mirror's Edge is its unique art style, which creates a clean and minimalist world with vibrant colors that make the game world feel alive. The game's visual design also includes some truly breathtaking environments that range from soaring skyscrapers to the gritty underbelly of the city, all of which are brought to life with impressive attention to detail.

The gameplay in Mirror's Edge is equally impressive, with a focus on free-running and parkour-style movement that allows players to navigate their environment in exciting and fluid ways. The game's control scheme is intuitive and easy to pick up, but mastering the various moves and techniques takes skill and practice. The level design is also top-notch, offering a wide range of challenges that require both quick reflexes and strategic thinking.

The camera mechanics in Mirror's Edge are also noteworthy, as they add to the game's immersive feel by following the character's movements in a natural way that makes the player feel like they are truly a part of the action. Whether running along walls, sliding under obstacles, or leaping across chasms, the camera always manages to keep up with the player, providing a seamless and immersive experience.

Overall, Mirror's Edge is an outstanding game that deserves all the praise it has received. From its immersive atmosphere and stunning visual design to its fluid gameplay and natural camera mechanics, it is a game that truly pushes the boundaries of what a first-person action game can achieve. If you're looking for a thrilling and immersive gaming experience, look no further than Mirror's Edge.

Definitely one of EA's more unique titles, and probably the best parkour-focused game you can find right now. If you're new to the series, play this and skip the largely disappointing Mirror's Edge Catalyst.

Gameplay-wise, the game feels pretty good to play once you get a handle on the controls. It can easily be played via a controller or keyboard+mouse; the latter option will give you a slight edge in gun battles, but since the game can be completed without touching a gun (except for one part where you have to shoot a police van) it doesn't matter what you use. The controls are awkward either way at first, but the more you play the more natural it'll start to feel. And once you get used to it, you'll probably wish that more games had similar mechanics. While Mirror's Edge might look like a FPS at some times, it's a platforming game above all else. Levels are presented in a linear fashion and you progress through like you would in any platforming game; using the enviornment to vault, swing, and crawl your way past obstacles. With only 9 levels, the game is on the short side...but it definitely has some replayability if you're looking to speedrun it. Gunplay may leave a little more to be desired; it feels clunky, and Faith can't carry ammo so when she disarms an enemy she can only use the rounds that are already in the gun. Apart from pistols and SMGs, guns will also considerably slow Faith down, no doubt an intentional move by DICE to emphasize that you sacrafice speed for power by picking up a weapon. Again, this doesn't matter much since guns are an entirely optional feature.

Graphically, it's a very pretty game. The game can be a little too bright sometimes, with it's pre-baked lighting and strong bloom effects, but overall it uses Unreal Engine 3 pretty well. The artstyle is fantastic; set in a near-futuristic dystopian city, the colorful city skylines make for a great view as you dance along the rooftops. Combined with a fantastic minimalistic HUD, the game presents many opportunities for gorgeous screenshots if you like to toy around with video game photography.

Moving on to presentation, Mirror's Edge has the same appeal that a cult movie would. The story is far from perfect with average voice acting, poor pacing, and a somewhat anticlimactic ending. That being said, it was still done effectively. If the story does anything good, it's world building. I found myself wanting to know more about the events leading up to the game's story, about the city, about Faith herself. The cutscenes will probably remind you of those old Esurance commercials, but they eventually grow on you. The soundtrack is pretty well done too, with the music from the final level being exceptionally good. Overall, the game is very obviously far from perfect and yet still charming in it's own unique way.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Mirror's Edge has a small but dedicated and enthusiastic fanbase for a reason. It's not for everybody and it's certainly not the best game in the world. In spite of that, it's aged well for an almost 10 year old game. It's got some of the best platforming mechanics I've seen in a first person game, although there's still a few frustrating trial-and-error segments. All in all, I think it's worth at least one playthrough...certainly more for a budding speedrunner. $20 might be asking a little much, but when it goes on sale it's a must buy in my opinion.

[i]Mirror's Edge[/i] is a relic of a seemingly bygone era, one [i]EA[/i] only recently resurrected. It was a more jolly time, one where online-only multiplayer-centric games infested with predatory monetization schemes weren't the norm, where [i]EA[/i] actually gave a damn and made fun single-player games like [i]The Saboteur[/i] or [i]Mercenaries 2[/i]. Were they the bestest games ever? No. But they were fun, and that's enough.

[h3][b][i]A woman's touch[/i][/b][/h3]
[i]"No stop signs, Speed limit, Nobody's gonna slow me down!"[/i] legendary words sung by the eternal raspy voice of [i]AC/DC[/i] vocalist Bon Scott. Thus, I'm sure he would also be as disappointed as I was with the existence of stop signs in [i]Mirror's Edge[/i], the [b]mandatory combat sections.[/b] Sure, once in a blue moon, I was let to get past the po-po with parkour or creatively dispose of them while keeping my momentum intact.

But, like finding anime without skimpy-clothed ladies with big bazongas, those moments were also rare. And my disdain for the game's combat stems from [b]not all enemies being created equal.[/b] Aside from one sniper section causing problems due to enemy placement, running past the pistol-carrying, shotgun, and sniper dudes was possible. But then came the big guns—the [b]assault rifle[/b] and [b]LMG boys[/b]. Oh, how I fricking hate them! Also, pause—[b]who da hell goes after a gunless runner with fricking LMGs!?[/b] I guess this is some futuristic thing I'm to present to understand.

Anyway, back on topic.

Unless the game allowed me to, there was no way I could progress without a fight. Trying always led to me having more holes than I originally started the game with. The only viable strategy was to stop and hide behind stuff in some secluded spot, wait for them to peek around the corner, and smack them. So, like the existence of diet water, I also don't understand why [i]Mirror's Edge[/i] has mandatory combat sections. I'll end my combat rant by playing devil's advocate—[b]I liked some of the combat gameplay's concepts.[/b] Sadly, it's bloody [i]raw![/i] and integrated in such a way that it completely sterilizes the parkour's flow during those later [i](mandatory combat)[/i] sections. Hopefully, the sequel improved it.

Aside from the combat, [b]the plot is another low point.[/b] Oh, look, Faith's (the main character) sister is being framed for murder. Ok... And I'm supposed to care about Faith and her sister because... tangerines? Stuff happens, then some other stuff happens. [i]Cool, I'm hooked now.[spoiler] /s [/spoiler][/i] There was nothing for me to get emotionally attached to—I was just thrust into the story and expected to care. So, I didn't. Lastly, the big baddie reveal, that [i]"surprise"[/i] twist, and the game's anticlimactic climax were all simply underwhelming.

I also wasn't a big fan of the 2D animated-style cutscenes. It clashed too much with the hyper-realistic graphics for my taste. Also, some quasi-cutscenes were rendered in-engine, so either they did this because of time constraints or budget cuts. Anyway, this is entirely a [i][b]me[/b][/i] problem; a friend who watched me play liked the cutscenes.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3105113687
But too much complaining, and I'll get wrinkles in weird places. Now, it's time I fanboy, as despite these blemishes, I really do [b]love[/b] [i]Mirror's Edge.[/i]

[h3][b][i]Simplicity hides Intricacy[/i][/b][/h3]
Theodore Roosevelt once said, [i]"Nothing in the world is worth having or worth doing unless it means effort, pain, difficulty."[/i] Clearly a [i]hardcore gamer[/i] and a man of refined taste who enjoys getting pegged by a [i]sophisticated[/i] gameplay system for simply moving your character. And look, I enjoy that too, especially if it comes from the buttocks of Lord Hidetaka Miyazaki, [i]praise be his name[/i]. But, unlike Teddy boy over there, I also appreciate the austere (yea, I do be googling new fancy words) things in life, like curvy waifus or husbandos, and find them instrumental if one is to have a well-balanced gamer diet. Now, [i]Mirror's Edge[/i] has none of that. But what it does have is the simple yet [i]tight[/i] parkour gameplay—dashing from obstacle to obstacle, chasing that next momentum [i]fix[/i], with the [i]going fast[/i] white stripes on the sides of my screen delivering a genuine sense of speed, as I perfectly chain my jumps, swings, rolls, slides, and wall runs while making my way to the objective, simply [b]breathtaking.[/b]

And it's the simplicity of the parkour system that truly makes it fun. There were [b]no convoluted button combos[/b] I had to memorize to execute any move. With a press of a single (sometimes two) button, I was soaring through the air. Or crashing right down to the ground, but we don't talk about that. [b]There's also slow-mo[/b], which, after [i]VR Chat[/i], is humanity's second greatest creation. And you might think it's in the game to make certain stunts easier to perform. [b]WRONG![/b] The sole purpose of this gameplay mechanic is to look cool while doing parkour.

As for where you'll be looking cool while you parkour, the levels are extremely linear. [b]But they do come with a systematic change in elevation, which I loved.[/b] It felt like the levels gave me freedom, like any object or wall was my plaything, ready to be stepped on by the soles of my weird runner shoes so I could reach the next checkpoint. Sadly, that's all a mirage born of the game loosening its extremely tight grip around my hand occasionally. [b]I really wish levels had a more hands-off approach to how I reached my goal.[/b] 

There's plenty of variety tho. From tall, white (in and out) glass-coated buildings with office spaces and rooftops with too many pipes to the sewers and metro station, [i]Mirror's Edge[/i] took me on a grand tour of [i]The City[/i] via its linear missions. I also love the game's visual style and use of its striking color pallet where whites dominate. It made other colors pop, effortlessly grabbing and directing my attention towards important landmarks I had to reach. However, one complaint I have is nothing really screams [i]the future![/i] in this seemingly futuristic-dystopian city.

But now I want to gush about how the game [b]guides the player.[/b]

I'm [i]pro-noHUD[/i] and love when the game's world, NPCs, etc., guides me, instead of ravishing my beautiful green eyes with its putrid UI clutter. And [i]DICE[/i] created something ingenious—[i]Runner Vision[/i]. I was guided towards my objective with only the color [b]red.[/b] 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3083619925
But, while I love the mechanic, [b]I'm also a stickler for immersion,[/b] so I turned it off. As a result, certain parts of the game, like the high-octane chase sequences or parrying enemy melee attacks, were more challenging. I had to think and act fast, or I was bread of the toasted kind. And since there was trial and error, this way, my immersion receptors get to feel the utmost pleasure, and I also satiated my masochistic urges—[b]it was a win-win![/b]

So, with all of that said, I hope the second part of my expertly written gigantic wall of text answers why I [b]love[/b] [i]Mirror's Edge[/i] so much. If it didn't, then let me paraphrase it. [i]Mirror's Edge's[/i] platforming gave me flirtation. [b]I like it, I love it, I want some more of it.[/b] Yes, the combat is undercooked and hurts the flow of the gameplay from time to time. But the parkour during my six-hour playthrough was so sublime, that in the wise words of me, [i]"The occasional pegging is a small price to pay if I get to parkour for 1/4th of a day."[/i]

i played this game for the first time in 2025 over a weekend because i picked it up on a sale and heard it was a classic

I thought the game had moments that were really cool, especially towards the end. In these moments I had movement nailed and I was moving fluidly through the game and feeling those parkour vibes

but I wish it was more of the game

too  much of the game had enemies and all they really did was force you to memorize a layout or die and try again repeatedly... i found it difficult to flow and improv with the mechanics, at least the first time seeing a new obstacle or enemy encounter. this seems like the kind of game you play a dozen times if it clicks with you like that

writing and story had me interested at first and then it totally lost me because it introduces characters and then never builds them up... by the end of the game i didn't really understand a lot of the motivations of the main characters and factions.

 then again, there was lore dumped throughout the game I mostly skipped, so maybe there was more there that I could've explored...  and again, maybe if I really got into it I would've uncovered all this stuff on subsequent playthroughs

i guess the point i'm trying to make here is that I feel like this game has some really cool environments, great art direction, and some revolutionary ideas about movement in a first person game, so it deserves to be remembered for that.

like all good art I feel like it's gotta have people who really like it, people who bounce off it, and other people who look and appreciate. I feel like the last. I appreciate a lot about this game, but I also don't really want to play it ever again lol 

highkey it's because i found a lot about movement awkward compared to modern games, and there was a few really frustrating moments where it really soured my experience overall. I enjoy challenge in games, but when I died it was usually from jank, so it was annoying vs. something I could learn from and improve with 

i liked a lot of the ideas overall though, and when it was cool, it was really cool. I'd recommend you try it, especially on the cheap

This was really fun to play. It mixes platform and puzzle elements with some light action (which can be mostly avoided, if you're all about the parkour). The movement felt smooth and responsive, but it still had its moments of clunkiness where it refused to jump where I was aiming.

The world looks large and impressive but you can only interact with maybe 10% of what you see. There's no true sense of freedom as nearly every level only has a single correct path to take, and other than a few collectables there's no real reason to explore. The gameplay is a bit trial and error too, I had to replay some of the same sections over and over until I'd mastered each exact jump.

I know this isn't a stealth game, but all the enemies can see through walls making any sort of tactical route planning impossible. "There she is!" they yell as they begin pelting your location with bullets, while you were hiding behind a truck 500 metres away with their backs to you. Luckily their aim is worse than a stormtroopers so they're rarely a problem.

The story is fine. It isn't terrible, it's just bland. You can tell who the bad guys are the moment you first meet them, then five hours later then game is all "aha, bet you didn't see this twist coming!" as you roll your eyes.

Graphically it has aged well very due to the stylish design they picked, a game from 2008 should have no right to look this good. If you're running an AMD card make sure you disable PhysX in the games options or suffer some horrendous frame drops.

It wasn't the parkour simulator that I was expecting, but its still a very fun game to play though once, even if it is a limiting experience.

OK, this game is from 2009. It doesn't look the best any more. That's where the criticisms stop.

For an EA game - there are no IAPs that I could find. There are zero bugs in the game, other than one where it didn't pre-load the map before the cutscene ended (I know that's not really a bug but I still put it here). The story is great and so is the sountrack.

I'd give this game a solid 8/10, and recommend people play it still today!
